rationale: I'm switching from Pearson correlations to tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariances on CC200. Abraham et al. 2017 found this the strongest classic connectivity pipeline on ABIDE. The reference mean is the log-Euclidean mean of the training subjects only, and each subject is whitened against it, which keeps subject-specific deviations and drops shared structure. ROIs that are all zero get an identity diagonal so the matrix logarithm stays finite.

Site differences in scanner and protocol are large, and scoring happens within each site, so I'm switching to per-site Riemannian re-centering. For each site, the tangent reference becomes the log-Euclidean mean of that site's covariances. It is computed without labels from all of that site's subjects, train and test (Zanini et al. 2018). This removes site-specific shared connectivity structure from the features before the linear classifier sees them. Sites with fewer than 5 subjects fall back to the global training mean.

I'm replacing the single CC200 model with an ensemble of four parcellations: CC200, CC400, AAL and Harvard-Oxford. Each atlas gets the same per-site re-centred tangent-space pipeline, and the ensemble averages their standardized logistic-regression decision scores. Different parcellations capture partly independent connectivity information, and Abraham et al. 2017 reported that combining atlases makes ABIDE classification more robust. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is not yet known.

I'm adding a second preprocessing strategy to the ensemble. Each of the four atlases now gets a model on GSR (`filt_global`) time series as well as the existing no-GSR (`filt_noglobal`) ones. Removing the global signal changes the covariance structure: it re-centres the correlation distribution and suppresses global and motion-related variance. So the tangent-space features from the two strategies should give partly independent views of the same connectivity, and the ensemble can gain from averaging their standardized scores. This is the same diversity argument that made the multi-atlas ensemble help. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is not yet known.

Sites have different scan lengths, TRs and noise levels, so after per-site re-centring their tangent features still differ in how widely they spread. I'm adding a label-free per-site, per-feature standardization of the tangent vectors, using all of each site's train and test subjects. Each site's variance is shrunk toward the pooled variance with weight k=10, in the spirit of ComBat, so small sites stay stable. This puts every site on a common scale before the linear classifier, which should help a within-site metric. I haven't run it, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm adding the Dosenbach160 atlas as a fifth member of the ensemble. Its 160 ROIs are spheres placed from meta-analyses of task fMRI and cover the default-mode, fronto-parietal, cingulo-opercular, sensorimotor, occipital and cerebellar networks. That makes it the least redundant option next to the existing data-driven atlases (CC200, CC400) and anatomical ones (AAL, HO). Adding parcellations was the biggest gain so far (round 3), and the existing code already handles all-zero ROIs, which this atlas can have in the cerebellum.

Right now the L2 strength is fixed at C=0.001. That value was chosen back in round 1, before per-site re-centring and standardization changed the scale and spread of the features. This round I pick C (one value shared by all four atlases) by grouped inner CV on the training fold, scoring the averaged ensemble with within-site AUROC. To keep this cheap, each atlas's training features are rotated into the basis of the training rows. This gives exactly the same L2-logistic solution, but needs only n×n fits instead of fits on ~77k features.

I'm adding a fifth, down-weighted ensemble member (weight 0.5 against 1.0 for each atlas) built on regional time-series features. Per ROI and across all four atlases, it uses: log amplitude relative to the subject's median ROI, as an ALFF proxy; and lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelation, as proxies for the low-frequency fraction (fALFF). Every atlas model z-scores each ROI and then uses a correlation-based tangent space, so this amplitude and spectral information never reaches the classifier at present. These features complement connectivity, and per-site standardization absorbs the TR and scanner differences.

Within-site AUROC only rewards separating cases from controls inside each site. Sites in ABIDE have different autism/control ratios, though, so the pooled logistic regression can partly fit site-level prevalence offsets. Those offsets also survive per-site centering, because each site's feature mean depends on its own class mix. This round I reweight training samples so each site counts as class-balanced, with weights normalized to mean 1 so the effective L2 strength stays the same. The classifier then learns within-site case-control contrasts instead of between-site prevalence. The Dev score for this change is not yet known.

With C=0.001, each atlas's L2 logistic regression is close to an independence rule: it projects onto the site-balanced class-mean difference and gives every one of the 6k–77k tangent edges a share of the weight. Fan & Fan (2008) showed that such rules in p≫n lose accuracy as noise accumulates over uninformative features. So I'm adding supervised edge screening inside each training fold: rank edges by their site-balanced mean difference, and keep the top fraction (5–100%) before fitting the logistic regression. Each atlas picks its fraction by grouped inner CV on the training fold, scored with within-site AUROC through a cheap mean-difference proxy. 100% is one of the options, so the model can fall back to the current behaviour.

ABIDE sites differ a lot, and the score is computed within each site. So edges whose effect shows up in every site should generalize better than edges driven by one or two large sites. I'm replacing the pooled mean-difference screening statistic with a per-edge DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis z-score across sites, which favours edges that replicate across sites. The inner-CV choice of how many edges to keep, including the keep-all fallback, stays as it is. The cheap proxy now projects onto the random-effects mean effect.

Each atlas currently uses a single screening fraction, chosen by argmax over a noisy 3-fold proxy CV, and that hard choice adds variance between folds. I'll instead fit the L2 logistic regression at each of the three best fractions from the inner CV and average their standardized scores. This acts as a soft threshold: the most strongly screened edges appear in every model and get more weight, while weaker edges are kept but count for less. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is not yet known.

With C=0.001 each atlas's logistic regression is close to a mean-difference projection, so its noise is dominated by a few large shared modes of the tangent edges, such as global connectivity, motion or arousal. This change finds those modes without labels, as the top principal components of all subjects' site-standardized features. It projects out the top k of them, and grouped inner CV picks k ∈ {0,1,2,4,8} jointly with the screening fraction (k=0 keeps the current behaviour), using closed-form updates so the per-k matrices are never built.

Last round, projecting out the top label-free principal components of the edges helped, but the inner CV could remove at most 8. ABIDE has 20 sites with very different protocols, plus motion, arousal, physiological noise and scan-length-dependent shrinkage, so the shared nuisance subspace is probably larger than that. This round I extend the candidate counts to {0,1,2,4,8,16,32}; the inner CV still picks the count, and ties still go to the smaller count, so the current behaviour remains available. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is not yet known.

After per-site standardization, the tangent-space edges are heavy-tailed. A few subjects with motion or other artifacts produce extreme values on many edges, and those values can dominate both the label-free nuisance PCs and the class-mean differences the heavily regularized logistic regression relies on. I'm winsorizing each site-standardized feature at ±3 SD before PC removal, screening and fitting, which limits those outliers without using labels or dropping any subject. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is not yet known.
